title: Knowledge Graph from Your Documents Using AI
summary:
The Problem With Cloud AI

Every token costs money. Every API call adds up. And your data goes to their servers.

The Local Alternative 

brew install ollama
ollama pull llama3.2
ollama serve

Now you have a GPT-4 level model running on your MacBook. Free. Private. Fast.

Real Code Example 

import requests

def ask_local_ai(question):
    r = requests.post(
        "http://localhost:11434/api/generate",
        json={"model": "llama3.2", "prompt": question, "stream": False}
    )
    return r.json()["response"]

# Works immediately, no API key needed
answer = ask_local_ai("Explain Docker in one paragraph")
print(answer)

title: I am writing a book: AI Agents with LangChain and LangGraph
summary:
I am writing a book: AI Agents with LangChain and LangGraph.

It is a practical developer book. 20 chapters in 5 parts, plus 6 complete projects:

  • Part I, Foundations: what agents are, setup, prompts, structured output
  • Part II, LangChain core: LCEL, chat models, tools, agents, memory
  • Part III, RAG done properly: chunking, vector stores, retrievers, quality
  • Part IV, LangGraph: state, routing, checkpointers, human in the loop, multi-agent systems
  • Part V, Production: guardrails, cost, evals, deployment with FastAPI and Docker

One rule I set for myself while writing it: no code goes into the book unless it has been run first, and no output is printed unless it came from a real run. If a chapter's example fails, the chapter does not ship.

The book is also the in-depth companion to the AI Agent Engineering course I am launching on LogicStack. Enrollment opens 1 November and is free until 15 November. Students who enroll in that window and complete the course will receive the full book PDF free, together with their certificate.

title: Self-hosting AstaBrief-8B for cited reports: check every bracket before anyone reads it
summary:
You have search over your own documents. Next comes a report with a reference after every claim, and the Allen Institute for AI (Ai2) released AstaBrief-8B for that writing step. The weights (the trained model file you download) are Apache 2.0, and the base is the Qwen team's Qwen3-8B. We ran it on one NVIDIA RTX A5000, a 24 GB card, and counted every reference it wrote.

Serving it is easy. One check in the code around it is not optional.

Decision one: the prompt is not yours to write

Ai2 trained the model on one fixed instruction file. The model card warns that swapping it may give "degraded or inconsistent behavior". So your code fills two blanks, the question and the excerpts, and keeps even the line "Note that the current year is 2025". No report stated the wrong year; whether it ranks 2025 papers as the latest work, we left untested.

Each excerpt carries a label: an ID, the first author, the year and a citation count (how many other papers cite it). The model copies it into square brackets after each claim, and should write "(LLM Memory)" when it relies on its own recollection.

Check the licence first. Apache 2.0 covers the weights only; the instruction file is CC-BY-NC-4.0, non-commercial. A paid product must clear that licence or write its own prompt in the same format, with the risk the card describes. Our SDK example ships no copy: it fetches the file from Ai2 at run time, under Ai2's terms.

Decision two: size the context, then let it batch

vLLM, the open-source program that loads a model onto the GPU and answers requests, treats AstaBrief as an ordinary Qwen3 model, with no custom code. Text is counted in tokens, about three quarters of a word each. The weights fill 16.4 GB of the 24 GB. We capped each request at 16,384 tokens (question, excerpts and report), the length of Ai2's final training round. The leftover memory holds two requests at that cap side by side. Our real requests were nearer 7,000 tokens, so about four fit.

Alone on the card, one report took 41.5 to 64.7 s, at roughly 39 tokens a second. Sending four is more telling.

Sent together, four reports took 85 s, against 209 s one after another. The first try missed that, through a bug of ours. Concurrency is how many requests a model may work on at once, and pinning a model to one GPU machine through our SDK set it to one. The four waited in line: 198 s, and one report vanished. One settings call raises the limit today. The vanished report revealed a second, unfixed bug. If the first token (the opening piece of the answer) takes over 3 minutes, the request closes empty with no error. The card still finishes a report nobody receives. The AstaBrief-8B test notes on inferencekey.com cover both, plus the workaround.

On your stack, test the concurrency limit at each layer, first-token time under load, and whether a timeout fails loudly.

Decision three: the label check is part of the pipeline

The 11 reports held 380 references, and 363 (95.5%) match an excerpt we sent. Good, and also the trap: the other 17 look just like the genuine ones.

Eight of the 11 reports cited 1 to 3 labels the prompt never contained. Part of them were our own excerpts with the label garbled. We sent [W4411306417 | Thapliyal et al. | 2025 | Citations: 45] and got back [4411306415 | Thapliyal et al. | 2025 | Citations: 111]. The rest were recalled papers, dressed in the same format and missing the tag ("(LLM Memory)" showed up once across 11 reports). Plain numeric IDs cured the missing W, not the wrong labels.

You know every label you sent, so the check is a set difference:

import re
sent = set(labels_in_prompt)                      # exactly as you formatted them
cited = set(re.findall(r"\[([^\[\]]+)\]", report))
unknown = cited - sent                            # flag before a human reads it

Two cleanups belong there too. Each report opens with an empty block, the slot Qwen3 models reserve for reasoning when that mode is enabled (turning it off was not part of our test). And the per-section summaries use slightly different markers than the prompt requests.

What the 95.5% does not tell you

The score proves each reference exists, not that claims are correct. We did not compare each sentence with its excerpt, yet drift turned up anyway. One report gave a paper 25 citations instead of 27, seven times over. Another turned "one eighth" of a cost into "1/4 cost". Ai2 flags the same weakness: the right study, cited for more than it found. Have a person review figures taken from excerpts.

The test was small: 4 questions, 15 OpenAlex abstracts each, inputs around 5,000 tokens. Ai2's quality score (87.0 out of 100, against 77.3 for plain Qwen3-8B) covers computer science questions only. We graded none of the reports, and ran no head-to-head against another model.

For the retrieval side, see our EmbeddingGemma 2 post on multimodal search. The full AstaBrief-8B write-up with the vLLM command, SDK example and per-request timings also has the complete citation tally.

Credit: Ai2's Asta team built, trained, evaluated and released AstaBrief and its prompt, using reports from Anthropic, OpenAI and DeepSeek models, with GPT-4.1 and DeepSeek-R1 as graders. The Qwen team made Qwen3-8B, the vLLM project serves it unchanged, Hugging Face hosts the weights, OpenAlex supplied the abstracts, and an AI Search video pointed us to the release. Our part: the SDK example, the run on our own cloud, the counting. Read the complete AstaBrief-8B report on inferencekey.com before you wire it into your stack.

title: logsloth reads the failing CI log so I don't have to
summary:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady

What I Built

I'm Anand Biju. I built logsloth, a small command line tool for the most boring part of my week: a red CI run.

The red X is never the bad part. The bad part is opening the log. You get a few hundred lines of checkout, cache restore, dependency install and cleanup, and somewhere in the middle is the one line that matters. The last line, Process completed with exit code 1, tells you nothing. So you scroll, you search for "error", you hit forty false matches, and ten minutes later you find out a package was missing.

logsloth does that scrolling. Give it a log file, pipe a command into it, or point it at a failed GitHub Actions run:

logsloth ci.log
npm test 2>&1 | logsloth
logsloth --gh https://github.com/owner/repo/actions/runs/1234567890

It prints a short card with four lines. CULPRIT is the real error line. WHERE is the file and line. WHY is one sentence on what went wrong. FIX is the next thing to do. Below that are the handful of log lines it used as evidence, with their original line numbers, so you can check it instead of trusting it. --md prints the same thing as Markdown for a PR comment, and --json is there for scripts.

Demo

These are all real runs on my machine. The first three use real logs from public projects, pulled with gh run view --log-failed.

A ruff-format pre-commit failure in psf/requests. The log is 284 lines and the run ends with about forty lines of git cleanup after the error. logsloth skips that and lands on the hook that failed:

A mypy error in pallets/flask. The error message wraps over three lines, and logsloth joins them back together:

A failing vitest assertion in vitejs/vite. The log is 653 lines. Here Gemma got distracted by a pnpm store prune line in the excerpt and suggested running it. The validator threw that out, and the card shows the built-in hint instead. The footer says so.

And one of the bundled examples, a pytest run where httpx was never installed:

Code

Anandb71 / logsloth

Reads a failing CI log so you don't have to. Code finds the evidence, a local Gemma explains it.

logsloth

A small CLI that reads a long failing CI, test, or build log and tells you the one thing that broke.

Code finds the evidence and states the facts. A local open-weight model (gemma3:1b via Ollama) only explains why it failed and suggests a fix. The model never sees the whole log.

Why

When CI goes red you get a few hundred lines of setup, cache restores, and cleanup, with the real error somewhere in the middle. Finding it is boring and you do it many times a week. logsloth does the scrolling for you and runs entirely on your machine, so private logs never leave it.

Install

pip install -e .

You also need Ollama and the default model:

ollama pull gemma3:1b

OLLAMA_HOST defaults to http://127.0.0.1:11434.

Usage

# a log file
logsloth path/to/ci.log
# piped from a local command
npm test 2>&1 | logsloth

# a failed
…
View on GitHub
ollama pull gemma3:1b
python3 -m venv .venv && . .venv/bin/activate
pip install -e .
logsloth examples/pytest_httpx.log

python -m pytest -q runs 47 tests. They never call the model or the network.

How I Built It

The rule I followed: code finds the facts, the model only explains them.

My first version let Gemma 3 1B write everything. It went badly. On a cargo error it wrote the literal text "one sentence: what broke" as the culprit. On a jest log it pointed at the test file instead of the file that was missing the import. On the real flask and requests logs it blamed git config and safe.directory, because the cleanup lines at the end of a GitHub log look like errors. That third one is why I stopped testing only on my own example logs.

So the work is split.

Triage is plain Python. It strips ANSI colours, including the literal ^[[36m that gh run view --log-failed leaves in, plus the timestamps and the jobstep prefix on every line. It folds repeated lines and then scores lines against known failure patterns: Python tracebacks and pytest E lines, Cannot find module, rust error[E...] with its --> location, mypy and ruff style path:line: error:, pre-commit hooks that print Failed, pip's No matching distribution, docker's failed to solve, and a few more. The final exit code 1 line can never be the main finding if anything else matched. CULPRIT and WHERE come straight from this step, so they are always lines that really are in the log.

Gemma only writes why and fix. It gets a short excerpt, between 6 and 15 lines in the runs above, not the whole log. The prompt only includes the rules that apply to this failure. When I listed every rule at once, the 1B model copied them, and suggested "install httpx using pip or npm".

Every answer gets checked. Why and fix are validated separately. They have to be non-empty and short. They can't repeat the prompt or the example. They can't tell a git story when the failure isn't about git. They have to name the real package, symbol or hook. If the fix says to install something, that name has to appear in the log. That check caught Gemma telling me to "include lodoc" when the log said lodash. A field that fails is replaced by a built-in hint for that error type, and the footer says which parts came from the model and which from the hint, for example why from gemma3:1b, fix from hint.

In my final runs over the seven logs, Gemma's why was kept in six and its fix in three. On the vite log both fields fell back to hints. On this shared, CPU-only box a call took between 1.9 and 34 seconds, and most were around 10.

It is standard-library Python. Ollama serves the model over HTTP on localhost. I built it this week with the Cursor CLI agent doing a lot of the typing, while I wrote the spec, ran it against real logs, and kept tightening the validator.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

CI logs are full of things you shouldn't paste into a hosted chatbot: internal hostnames, paths, package names from a private registry, sometimes a token someone forgot to mask. With an open-weight model on my own machine, the log stays here. Nothing gets uploaded, there's no API key to manage, and running it a hundred times a day costs nothing.

It also changed how I built it. A 1B model running locally is fast and cheap enough to call on every failure, but it is wrong often enough that I had to treat its output as a suggestion to check, not an answer. Because I control the prompt, the temperature, the retry and the validation, I could build that checking around it. Swapping in a different model is one flag, --model.

The Lazy Payoff

Before: open the run, expand the failed step, scroll past setup, search for "error", skip the false matches, find the real line, then work out which file it means.

After: logsloth --gh . I read four lines, then check the evidence lines if I don't believe them. On the 653-line vite log the card had the failing spec file and line, and the expected and received values, in the evidence block. I didn't have to open the log.

Prize Categories

Best Use of Gemma. logsloth runs Gemma 3 1B (gemma3:1b) locally through Ollama. It writes the why and fix, and the validator decides which of its answers to keep.

title: Teaching an AI assistant to forget a deleted Stripe customer
summary:
Here is a small billing horror story.

A customer asks to be deleted. Someone clicks delete in Stripe. A week later your AI assistant is still happily telling people what that customer pays and which invoice is open. It sounds completely sure. It is completely wrong.

Nothing crashed. The assistant just kept a memory of something that no longer exists.

I wanted to fix that for Stripe. So for Mergetober I built a connector for Cognee. The code lives in PR #394 for issue #4547.

Billing data is a good test for a connector. Nothing in it stands alone. A charge belongs to an invoice, an invoice to a subscription, a subscription to a customer. If a connector loses those links, the assistant loses the story.

What it does

Cognee turns documents into a knowledge graph that an agent can search. The connector feeds it from Stripe. It reads customers, subscriptions, invoices, charges, products and disputes. Then:

  • Every object becomes a short document.
  • Related objects stay connected. A customer, its subscription, the invoice, the charge and the dispute can all be reached from each other.
  • Later runs read only what changed.
  • Anything you delete in Stripe is forgotten. 
await cognee.remember(
    stripe_source(),  # key and account come from the environment
    dataset_name="stripe",
    primary_key="id",
    write_disposition="merge",
)

It never reads card numbers or payment methods. Each document is built from a short list of allowed fields, not from the raw object. A field Stripe adds next year cannot sneak in by accident. Email, phone and metadata are off unless you ask for them.

Two choices I changed my mind about

Links. My plan was to treat Stripe rows as a relational table and let Cognee build the links from foreign keys. Then I checked. The staging tables dlt writes to SQLite have no foreign keys at all, even when you declare them. So the links would never appear.

The fix was simpler. Every document lists the things it belongs to: customer:cus_..., subscription:sub_..., product:prod_.... Cognee stores those as shared nodes. Two documents that share a node are connected. No guessing, and no model involved.

Changes. Stripe's list calls can only filter by creation date. That sounds fine until someone pays an old invoice. The invoice was created last month, so a date filter never sees it again.

So later runs read Stripe's events instead. One request asks what happened since last time. Then only the objects named in those events are fetched again. If nothing happened it costs one request. If the events are older than Stripe keeps them, the connector lists everything again and compares.

The real test

First I tested against a fake Stripe. 62 tests, no network. But a fake only proves what you thought to fake.

So I made a free Stripe test account, seeded it with three customers, and gave the connector a read-only key that can look but not touch.

The first sync took in 25 objects across all six types and Cognee built the graph with OpenAI. I asked which customers have unpaid invoices. The answer was Charliecorp, with an open invoice for $120.00. I asked which customers have a disputed charge and what plan they are on. It followed the trail from the dispute to the charge to the customer to the subscription to the plan and answered fraudulent, needs response, Pro plan at $49 a month.

Then I synced again without changing anything. One request. Nothing written.

Then I renamed a customer and deleted another straight from the Stripe dashboard. The next sync made three requests, wrote one object and forgot one. The deleted customer vanished from the documents and from the graph. The renamed one showed up under its new name.

That is the behaviour I wanted.

The bug only a real account could find

My first real run printed every charge without a link to its invoice.

My fake Stripe gave charges an invoice field. The real one does not. In the API version I pin (2025-03-31) a charge no longer says which invoice it paid. Instead the invoice lists its payments, and you have to ask for them. My tests passed on imaginary data and missed it completely.

The fix links the two through the payment they share. The invoice and the charge now both belong to the same payment_intent node. The fake now behaves like the real thing, so a test would catch this next time. A review pass flagged a second risk. A dispute's events name only the dispute, so the charge's disputed flag could go stale. The connector now refreshes the charge too.

Try it

The seed script and the example live in packages/connector/stripe/. Stripe's test mode is free and needs no business verification. Create a restricted key with read access, run the seed once, then rename and delete things in the dashboard between runs.

If you point it at your own account I would love to hear what breaks.

title: Auto‑Generate Security Incident Heatmaps from CSV with LLM Prompts
summary:
A recent internal audit of a Fortune 500 SOC showed that analysts spent an average of 42 minutes per day manually filtering CSV logs before they could draw a heatmap of suspicious activity. ## 1. Pull raw events into a structured CSV

Security devices, firewalls, IDS/IPS, and endpoint agents, export logs in CSV format. A typical row contains a timestamp, source IP, destination IP, protocol, and a numeric risk score.

# Example: extract the last 24 h from a Palo Alto CSV export
awk -F',' '$1 >= "$(date -d "-24 hours" +%Y-%m-%d)"' panos_traffic.csv > recent.csv


plaintext

The resulting recent.csv is the only input the LLM will ever see. Keep the column order consistent; rename ambiguous headers to ts,src_ip,dst_ip,proto,score. Takeaway: Standardize every CSV export to the same header set before feeding it to a language model. ## 2. Prompt the LLM to produce a heatmap script

Large language models excel at turning plain text specifications into runnable code. The prompt below asks the model to generate a Python script that reads recent.csv and outputs a heatmap PNG showing incident density by hour and source subnet.

You are a security automation expert. Write a Python 3 script that:
- reads recent.csv (columns: ts,src_ip,dst_ip,proto,score)
- parses ts as ISO‑8601, groups events by hour (0‑23) and by the first two octets of src_ip (e.g., 10.0, 192.168)
- sums the score for each bucket
- creates a heatmap where the X‑axis is hour, Y‑axis is src subnet, and color intensity is the summed score
- saves the figure as heatmap.png using matplotlib and seaborn
- includes a command‑line argument `--output` to change the file name

When you paste this prompt into a tool like OpenAI's ChatGPT or Claude, the model returns a complete script within seconds. Review the code for any hard‑coded paths, then run it directly. Takeaway: A single, well‑crafted prompt replaces dozens of manual copy‑paste steps and yields production‑ready code. ## 3. Execute the generated script in a CI pipeline

Integrate the script into a GitHub Actions workflow so the heatmap updates with every new CSV upload. Below is a minimal workflow that triggers on a new file in the logs/ directory.

name: Heatmap Generation
on:
 push:
 paths:
 - 'logs/*.csv'
jobs:
 build:
 runs-on: ubuntu-latest
 steps:
 - uses: actions/checkout@v3
 - name: Set up Python
 uses: actions/setup-python@v5
 with:
 python-version: '3.11'
 - name: Install deps
 run: pip install pandas matplotlib seaborn
 - name: Generate heatmap
 run: |
 python generate_heatmap.py --output heatmap.png
 - name: Upload artifact
 uses: actions/upload-artifact@v3
 with:
 name: heatmap
 path: heatmap.png


markdown

The workflow runs in under two minutes for a 500 KB CSV, producing a PNG that can be attached to a ticket or posted to Slack. Takeaway: Automate the script execution with CI/CD to guarantee fresh visual summaries without manual intervention. ## 4. Visual tweaks that matter to responders

Analysts often complain that heatmaps are either too dark or lack context. Add these three tweaks to the generated script before committing:

  1. Log‑scale color map – prevents high‑score outliers from flattening the rest of the plot.

    import numpy as np
sns.heatmap(matrix, cmap='viridis', norm=matplotlib.colors.LogNorm())

  2. Overlay event count – a small white number on each cell shows raw incident volume.

    for i in range(matrix.shape[0]):
for j in range(matrix.shape[1]):
plt.text(j+0.5, i+0.5, int(count_matrix[i, j]),
ha='center', va='center', color='white', fontsize=8)

  3. Dynamic title – embed the date range pulled from the CSV.

    start = df['ts'].min().date()
end = df['ts'].max().date()
plt.title(f'Incident Heatmap {start} → {end}')

These three lines turn a generic PNG into a decision‑ready artifact that responders can reference while triaging. Takeaway: Small visual refinements dramatically increase the heatmap's operational value. ## 5. Validate and iterate with a feedback loop

After the first deployment, collect two metrics for the next week:

  • Mean Time to Visual Insight (MTVI): time from CSV arrival to heatmap availability. - False‑negative heat zones: count of high‑risk periods that the heatmap failed to highlight. If MTVI stays above 5 minutes, revisit the CI step that copies the CSV into the repo; a direct S3 sync can shave seconds. If false‑negative zones appear, adjust the grouping granularity from /16 subnets to /24. bash # Example: switch to /24 subnets in the generated script src_subnet = '.'.join(src_ip.split('.')[:3])

Iterating on the script is cheap because the LLM can regenerate the modified section on demand. Takeaway: Treat the heatmap pipeline as a feedback‑driven product; small parameter tweaks yield measurable security gains. ---

Deploy the prompt, script, and GitHub Action today, then schedule a 15‑minute review tomorrow to confirm the PNG appears in your incident channel. This single change cuts manual parsing time from dozens of minutes to under a minute per shift.

title: Rewriting a JSON File in Place Let My Reader See It Half-Written: Temp File, fsync, os.replace and Three Traps
summary:
Now and then my page-building script died with JSONDecodeError: Expecting value: line 1 column 1 (char 0), reading a JSON index of video clips that looked perfectly fine when I opened it a second later. Another script rewrote that index every time a new clip landed, and most of the time the two got along.

Nothing was corrupting the file. The reader was opening it during the short window when the writer had emptied it and not yet finished filling it back in.

Disclosure: I make an Android camera app. Nothing below uses its code or describes how it stores anything. Every script here ran on one Linux machine with Python 3.10.12, in a throwaway folder, and the outputs are pasted unedited.

What the tests showed:

  • open(path, 'w') empties the file before you write a byte. A reader polling the file while it was rewritten failed far more often than it succeeded.
  • A crash in the middle of that write loses the old version too. Killing the writer left a fragment on disk and nothing to fall back to.
  • Write a temporary file next to the real one, then os.replace it into place. With that change the same reader did not see a single broken file.
  • The pattern has three traps around it: a temp folder on another filesystem, file permissions, and symlinks. Each one showed up in a few lines of test code.

Test one: a reader polling a file that is rewritten in place

The writer dumps a list of clip names into index.json with the usual with open(PATH, 'w'). A thread reads and parses the same file in a loop for as long as the writer is busy.

import json, os, sys, threading, time

PATH = "index.json"
clips = [{"name": "clip_%05d.mp4" % i, "bytes": 1000 + i} for i in range(20000)]

def write_in_place(n):
    for _ in range(n):
        with open(PATH, "w") as f:
            json.dump({"clips": clips}, f)

def read_loop(stop, seen):
    while not stop.is_set():
        try:
            with open(PATH) as f:
                json.load(f)
            seen["ok"] += 1
        except json.JSONDecodeError as e:
            seen["bad"] += 1
            seen.setdefault("first", str(e))

write_in_place(1)
stop, seen = threading.Event(), {"ok": 0, "bad": 0}
t = threading.Thread(target=read_loop, args=(stop, seen))
t.start()
write_in_place(200)
stop.set(); t.join()
print("good reads:", seen["ok"], "| failed reads:", seen["bad"])
print("first error:", seen.get("first"))

good reads: 162 | failed reads: 904
first error: Expecting value: line 1 column 1 (char 0)

Two different failures show up across runs. char 0 means the reader opened the file after open(..., 'w') had truncated it and before any data arrived, so it parsed an empty file. On another run the first error was Unterminated string, which means the reader caught the file partly written. Either way, the reader got a file that was not any valid version of the index.

The exact counts change from run to run, because they depend on how the two threads happen to interleave. What stayed the same across every run I did is that failures were common, not rare. A bigger file means more time between the truncation and the last byte, which gives a reader more chances to land in between.

Test two: the writer dies halfway

A separate process opens the index for writing, writes the first half of a new version, flushes it, and then sits there. The parent kills it with SIGKILL, which stands in for a crash or an out-of-memory kill.

import json, os, signal, subprocess, sys, time

PATH = "index.json"
json.dump({"clips": ["clip_00001.mp4"]}, open(PATH, "w"))
print("before:", os.path.getsize(PATH), "bytes, valid JSON")

child = r'''
import json, time
f = open("index.json", "w")
f.write('{"clips": ["clip_00001.mp4", "clip_00002.mp4"')
f.flush()
time.sleep(30)
f.write("]}")
'''
p = subprocess.Popen([sys.executable, "-c", child])
time.sleep(1)
p.send_signal(signal.SIGKILL)
p.wait()
print("writer exit status:", p.returncode)
print("after:", repr(open(PATH).read()))
try:
    json.load(open(PATH))
except json.JSONDecodeError as e:
    print("JSONDecodeError:", e)

before: 29 bytes, valid JSON
writer exit status: -9
after: '{"clips": ["clip_00001.mp4", "clip_00002.mp4"'
JSONDecodeError: Expecting ',' delimiter: line 1 column 46 (char 45)

The old index was valid before the child started. Once the child opened the file in 'w' mode, the old version was gone, and the new one did not finish. Any program that reads this file after the crash gets the fragment.

This is the case that hurts more than the torn read, because retrying does not help. The reader in test one could try again a moment later and succeed. Here the file stays broken until something rewrites it.

The fix: build the new version beside the old one, then swap

The idea is that the real path should not point at a half-built file at any moment. Write the complete new version to a temporary file in the same folder, make sure it is on disk, and then rename it over the real name in one step.

Python's documentation for os.replace describes the step that makes this work: "If successful, the renaming will be an atomic operation (this is a POSIX requirement)." A reader that opens the path gets the old file or the new file, not a mixture.

import json, os, tempfile

def atomic_write_json(path, obj):
    path = os.path.realpath(path)
    folder = os.path.dirname(path)
    fd, tmp = tempfile.mkstemp(dir=folder, prefix=".tmp-", suffix=".json")
    try:
        with os.fdopen(fd, "w") as f:
            json.dump(obj, f)
            f.flush()
            os.fsync(f.fileno())
        try:
            os.chmod(tmp, os.stat(path).st_mode & 0o7777)
        except FileNotFoundError:
            os.chmod(tmp, 0o644)
        os.replace(tmp, path)
    except BaseException:
        try:
            os.unlink(tmp)
        except FileNotFoundError:
            pass
        raise
    dfd = os.open(folder, os.O_RDONLY)
    try:
        os.fsync(dfd)
    finally:
        os.close(dfd)

Line by line, the choices that matter:

  • os.path.realpath(path) resolves symlinks first. Trap three below shows why.
  • tempfile.mkstemp(dir=folder, ...) creates the temp file in the same folder as the target, not in the system temp folder. Trap one shows why.
  • f.flush() then os.fsync(...) pushes the new bytes to the disk before the rename, so the swap does not publish a name that points at data still sitting in a buffer.
  • The os.chmod copies the old file's permission bits onto the temp file. Trap two shows why.
  • On any exception the temp file is deleted, so a failed write does not leave clutter behind. A process killed outright skips that handler, so a fixed prefix like .tmp- also makes leftovers easy to find and sweep later.
  • After the rename, the folder itself is opened and fsynced. A rename is a change to the folder, not to the file, and this asks the operating system to write that change out as well.

Here is the reader from test one again, pointed at the new writer:

import json, threading
from atomic_write import atomic_write_json

PATH = "index.json"
clips = [{"name": "clip_%05d.mp4" % i, "bytes": 1000 + i} for i in range(20000)]

def read_loop(stop, seen):
    while not stop.is_set():
        try:
            with open(PATH) as f:
                json.load(f)
            seen["ok"] += 1
        except json.JSONDecodeError:
            seen["bad"] += 1

atomic_write_json(PATH, {"clips": clips})
stop, seen = threading.Event(), {"ok": 0, "bad": 0}
t = threading.Thread(target=read_loop, args=(stop, seen))
t.start()
for _ in range(200):
    atomic_write_json(PATH, {"clips": clips})
stop.set(); t.join()
print("good reads:", seen["ok"], "| failed reads:", seen["bad"])

good reads: 3034 | failed reads: 0

Every read parsed.

Trap one: the temp file lives on a different filesystem

It is tempting to call tempfile.mkstemp() with no folder and let it pick the system temp directory. The Python documentation for os.replace warns that "The operation may fail if src and dst are on different filesystems." On this machine /tmp and the project folder are on different disks, so that is easy to show:

import os, tempfile

fd, tmp = tempfile.mkstemp(dir="/tmp", suffix=".json")
os.write(fd, b'{"clips": []}')
os.close(fd)
print("temp file:", tmp)
print("same filesystem?", os.stat("/tmp").st_dev == os.stat(".").st_dev)
try:
    os.replace(tmp, "index.json")
except OSError as e:
    print(type(e).__name__, e.errno, e.strerror)
finally:
    if os.path.exists(tmp):
        os.unlink(tmp)

temp file: /tmp/tmp1c9a6qvr.json
same filesystem? False
OSError 18 Invalid cross-device link

Error 18 is EXDEV. A rename cannot move data between filesystems; it only relinks a name inside one. shutil.move, for example, falls back to copying when a rename fails across filesystems, and a copy is exactly the non-atomic write you were trying to avoid.

Whether /tmp shares a disk with your data depends on the machine, which is what makes this trap nasty: the same code can pass on a laptop and fail on a server, or the other way around. Creating the temp file in the target's own folder removes the question.

Trap two: the new file quietly gets different permissions

title: How to auto-trade the calls from a Discord trading server (without a bot token)
summary:
How to auto-trade the calls from a Discord trading server (without a bot token)

Most people who trade from a Discord server do the same thing: a call lands, the phone buzzes, they open the broker app, type the ticket, and get filled somewhere between thirty seconds and never. The server is the signal. The human is the bottleneck.

I spent a while trying to close that gap with my own code, and I build Nyria now, which does it as a product. This post covers what I learned the hard way with a self-written bot, and then the setup I use today, which takes no bot token, no server and no code. Disclosure up front so you can weigh the rest.

The do-it-yourself route, and where it leaks

The obvious plan: create a Discord application, get a bot token, invite the bot to the server, listen for on_message, parse the text, hit the broker API.

@client.event
async def on_message(message):
    if message.channel.id != CALLS_CHANNEL:
        return
    text = message.content or embed_text(message)
    side, ticker = parse(text)
    broker.place_order(ticker, side, qty)

It works for an afternoon. Then the problems arrive in this order:

  1. Permissions. You can only invite a bot to a server where you have Manage Server. A paid room you merely belong to will not let you add one, and reading it through your own user account is against Discord's terms and gets accounts banned.
  2. Formats. Callers post plain text, embeds, screenshots, quoted tweets. Your parse() grows a case for each and still misses the one written at 9:31 in a hurry.
  3. Noise. The same channel carries "nice fill", questions and someone's lunch. Every false positive is a real order.
  4. Hosting. The listener has to be awake at 3 AM when the crypto call hits. Laptops sleep. Free tiers restart.
  5. Exits. An entry is one message; the exit is another, hours later, in different words. Matching them against what the account is actually holding is the part most home-grown bots never finish.

None of these are hard individually. Together they are a part-time job that pays nothing until the trading does.

The setup I use now

Nyria has its own Discord bot. You invite it to a server you run and it asks for one permission, View Channels. There is no token to manage, nothing to host, and it never reads messages on your personal account. The steps, in the order the app walks you through them:

1. Connect Discord. Integrations, Discord card, Connect Discord. Discord asks for two scopes: identify, to map your Discord user to your Nyria account, and guilds, to list the servers you belong to. That is all.

2. Create a strategy with Discord as the source. On the channel step, select Invite bot to server. You need Manage Server in that server, which is the same rule as any Discord bot. If the caller you follow runs the room and you don't, the fix is at the end of this post.

3. Pick the channel and narrow it. One channel per strategy. Add an Author filter when several people post in the same channel, and a Keyword filter such as ALERT when calls share the channel with chatter. The preview shows the last 25 messages so you can see exactly what the bot will read.

4. Teach it the format from real messages. On the strategy's Alert format card, assign one past message to each trade type you enable: long entry, long exit, shorts if you trade them. Nyria shows what each message would have traded. If it reads one wrong, assign a different message or change the strategy before any bot runs. Nobody in the channel changes how they write.

5. Deploy on paper first. Deploy bot, choose Nyria Paper, set a budget per entry. Paper is free and needs no card. Let a few calls fire and read each fill on the bot's Logs tab, next to the message that caused it.

6. Then the broker. When the paper fills track the posts, deploy a second bot on your Alpaca, Tradier, tastytrade or Charles Schwab account with the same sizing. The next message that passes the filters places a trade.

What a call needs to contain

A ticker, a direction and an action. The wording is the caller's own. These all read:

Entering BTC long at support
BTO AAPL 345c 11/20 @ 12.50
long SPY
STC SPY 772c
sold half, trimming the rest at 780

Embeds are read first, then a quoted tweet, then the plain text. A message with no size, no price and no venue, like long SPY, is still a complete alert: the strategy and the bot supply the size (budget per entry), the order type (market, or limit at the alert's price if it names one) and the account.

How exits work

Nothing waits at the broker between messages. An exit is an exit alert: STC SPY 772c, or a plain "sold" with no contract, closes what the entry opened in the same instrument, matched against what the bot is holding. The next move is always the next message.

This is the design choice that made my own bot hard: it forces you to think of the channel as the whole state machine, which is also why it holds up.

What to watch on the Logs tab

Every order sits beside the alert that caused it, with the receive time and the fill time to the millisecond. Every refusal does too, written in plain words: the budget per entry is lower than one unit costs, the message passed the filters but named no ticker, the market is closed for that asset. Nothing is ordered on a refusal. Read the log for a week on paper and you will know exactly which messages in that channel are trades and which are talk.

If you don't run the server

The bot can't join a paid Discord you only belong to, and nothing legitimate can. Two honest options:

  • Ask the caller to publish their calls as a strategy on Nyria. Members subscribe and deploy a bot in their own broker account; the caller gets paid per tier, through Nyria, Stripe or Whop. Many callers want this once they see their members are retyping every entry.
  • Run your own server for your own alerts: TradingView webhooks, a script, your own posts. Same setup, no permission problem.

Where to start

Make a free account at nyria.io, create a strategy with Discord as the source, point it at a channel you run and deploy a paper bot. No card, no token, no server to keep awake. When the paper fills match what the channel posts, you'll know whether it is worth pointing at a real account.

This is the design choice that made my own bot hard: it forces you to think of the channel as the whole state machine, which is also why it holds up.

What to watch on the Logs tab

Every order sits beside the alert that caused it, with the receive time and the fill time to the millisecond. Every refusal does too, written in plain words: the budget per entry is lower than one unit costs, the message passed the filters but named no ticker, the market is closed for that asset. Nothing is ordered on a refusal. Read the log for a week on paper and you will know exactly which messages in that channel are trades and which are talk.

If you don't run the server

The bot can't join a paid Discord you only belong to, and nothing legitimate can. Two honest options:

  • Ask the caller to publish their calls as a strategy on Nyria. Members subscribe and deploy a bot in their own broker account; the caller gets paid per tier, through Nyria, Stripe or Whop. Many callers want this once they see their members are retyping every entry.
  • Run your own server for your own alerts: TradingView webhooks, a script, your own posts. Same setup, no permission problem.

Where to start

Make a free account at nyria.io, create a strategy with Discord as the source, point it at a channel you run and deploy a paper bot. No card, no token, no server to keep awake. When the paper fills match what the channel posts, you'll know whether it is worth pointing at a real account.

title: I Built a Tool to Check Whether a GitHub Repository Actually Works

I Built Clone to Confidence

Have you ever cloned a GitHub repository only to discover that it doesn't run as expected?

Missing dependencies, broken tests, incomplete configuration, and undocumented assumptions can make repository verification frustrating.

I built Clone to Confidence to help developers identify these problems systematically.

What It Does

Clone to Confidence is an offline-first repository auditing tool designed to make verification more explicit and reproducible.

Key features include:

  • Eight deterministic audit checks
  • PASS, FAIL, and WARN evidence
  • Confidence scoring
  • Machine-readable JSON reports
  • A local web dashboard
  • Explicit Docker and test verification
  • Create-only safe fixes

Why I Built It

I wanted to explore how developers could verify repository readiness instead of relying entirely on README instructions or assumptions.

The goal is to make repository problems easier to identify and audit.

title: Agent Graph Engineering, Part 2: Split the Services, and Know Where the Line Goes
summary:
TL;DR Put your product's domain in one service and your agent graph in another, and draw the line at state ownership rather than at anything that sounds like a layer. The agent owns execution state, which is a LangGraph checkpoint nobody can rebuild by hand. The backend owns the record, which is what a page reload needs. Updates travel one way, agent to backend, over a generated WebSocket client. The payoff is not tidiness, it is that a node is a function you can call with a state you invented, while the same decision inside a socket consumer needs a connection and a user before it will run at all.

Part 1 listed the stack and said, in one line, to keep business logic out of the agent. That line does a lot of work and deserves its own post, because it is the decision that is nearly free this month and expensive in a year, and because "split it into two services" is useless advice until somebody tells you where the cut goes.

What the merged version looks like

I have shipped the single-service version. It does not fail dramatically. It degrades, in a way that is hard to argue with in a code review because every individual step was reasonable.

It goes something like this. Your agent needs to know whether a customer is on the paid plan, so the prompt grows a line about entitlements. Then billing adds an annual tier, and now the prompt is wrong in a way no test catches, because the prompt is a string and nothing validates strings against your billing model. Meanwhile a graph node needs the ticket's history, so it reads the ORM directly, and now your graph cannot run in a test without a database and fixtures. Six months later somebody asks whether the agent can be deployed separately, because the model calls are slow and the web workers are blocked waiting on them, and the answer is no, not without unpicking all of it.

The two failure directions are worth naming separately, because they feel different while you are in them. Business rules leak into prompts, where they cannot be type-checked or unit-tested. Graph concerns leak into models, where a tickets table starts carrying columns about node execution. Neither side can be tested alone by then, which is the point at which the split stops being a refactor and becomes a rewrite.

The test you cannot write

That last sentence is the one that matters, so here is what it looks like from inside.

In the merged version the agent's decision happens inside the socket consumer, in a method that has already authenticated the user, loaded the conversation and written a row. To assert that a particular message routes to a particular capability, you have to arrive at that line the way a user does: open a connection, authenticate it, seed a session and a conversation, and let the whole thing run until the part you care about executes. The assertion is one line. Everything above it is travel.

The mocks are worse than the setup. Because the model is reached through that object rather than across a boundary, there is no single place to stub it. You stub each collaborator where it happens to be used, so the fakes multiply with the call graph instead of with the number of seams. A suite like that gains patches faster than it gains assertions, and past a certain density nobody can tell you which parts are still being exercised and which are being asserted against a mock of themselves.

A graph node does not have that problem, and not because graphs are virtuous. It is because a node is a function from state to state. You build the state you want, call it, and look at what came back.

async def test_knowledge_base_branch_grounds_the_answer() -> None:
    thread = "kb-branch"
    with mock_openai(CLASSIFY, SEARCH_KB, ANSWER_FROM_KB) as route:
        state = (
            await SupportGraph()
            .compile(checkpointer())
            .ainvoke({"context": ticket()}, config=config(thread))
        )

    assert route.call_count == 3
    assert isinstance(state["decision"], SearchKnowledgeBase)
    # The retrieval step ran and fed the answer agent.
    assert state["kb_snippets"]
    assert any("kb-002" in snippet for snippet in state["kb_snippets"])

That is the whole test, not an excerpt. The three capitalized names are canned model replies declared at the top of the file. There is no socket to open and nobody to log in, because the node never needed either. The only thing faked is the model's HTTP response, which is the one real boundary in the picture, and everything underneath it runs: three model calls, a retrieval step, a routing decision, and an answer that had to cite what retrieval handed back.

So the argument for splitting is narrower and more useful than "separation of concerns". It was never about tidiness. It was about being able to call the thing.

The cut is about state, not layers

The instinct is to split by technology or by layer: an API tier, a service tier, maybe a cache in front. That produces a diagram your architect likes and a boundary that leaks within a month, because layers are not what is actually different about these two things.

What is actually different is the kind of state each one holds.

The agent owns execution state: which node runs next, the current channel values, the payload of a pending interrupt. In LangGraph that is a checkpoint, and it lives in Postgres. The important property is that you cannot rebuild it by hand. If you lose a checkpoint, you have not lost a row you could recompute from other rows. You have lost the ability to resume, because reconstructing it means reimplementing LangGraph's execution model, and you are not going to do that. Resumption is the whole mechanism behind human approval, so this state is load-bearing in a way ordinary application state is not.

The backend owns the record: messages, ticket events, and the two things a page reload needs to find, which are a drafted reply waiting for approval and a proposed tool call. None of those are copies of graph state. They exist because a browser cannot ask the agent what is currently waiting, and because a stored approval row is what lets the approval card come back after a refresh.

Once the line is drawn there, a lot of smaller questions answer themselves. Permissions, billing, and user records are obviously the backend's, because they are the record. Prompts, tools, and routing are obviously the agent's, because they are execution. The service the agent exposes has one job, and the service your product lives in never imports LangGraph.

In the reference implementation it comes out as three services:

Service Owns Port
backend/ users, tickets, the thread as a person reads it 8000
agent/ graphs, tools, checkpoints, the model's memory 8001
web/ nothing; it renders what the other two generate 5173

Three services and four processes, because a run is driven by a worker rather than by whichever web process accepted the request. That worker is the backend's own code pulling from a queue, so it owns nothing the table does not already list.

The agent is internal. Only the backend connects to it, never a browser, and that matters more than it looks. The approval gate lives inside the graph, so anything that can open a socket on the agent can both propose a tool call and approve it. Network isolation is the primary control there and a shared token is the second one, which is why the token is optional in a fresh clone and not optional anywhere real.

Two threads, not one

I got this wrong the first time, and the symptom was confusing enough to be worth the detail.

There are two conversation histories in a system like this, and they are not the same object.

One is the thread as a person reads it: an ordered list of events you can render, paginate, and show to a customer. That is rows, and it belongs to the backend.

The other is the thread as the model remembers it, which in Pydantic AI is its own message history. That is not a list of rows. It carries tool calls and their results, the shapes of previous structured outputs, and the sequencing the model needs to behave consistently on the next turn. Flattening it into "a list of messages" throws away exactly the parts that make the next call work.

I first gave that model memory its own table, filled by a background job once the message itself had been saved. Two copies of one thread, written by two processes at two different times, which is the shape of a problem whether or not you have hit it yet. The gap between those writes is not a rare crash window either, which is what I had told myself. It is ordinary operation: the job queues, it retries, occasionally it does not arrive, and the write that already succeeded neither knows nor cares. When the two disagreed, neither had been derived from the other, so neither could be rebuilt. There was no correct recovery, only a choice about which copy to believe.

The fix was to stop treating it as a second source of truth. The model's memory now rides on the graph's state, so the checkpointer that already persists a parked run persists the memory too. One write, one thing to lose. And when a lane has nothing remembered yet, it starts from the record the backend sends, which quietly turns the memory into a cache over the record rather than a peer of it. Lose a checkpoint now and what you lose is the shape of past tool calls, not the conversation.

That is the test I would apply to any state you are tempted to put on the agent side. If losing it means losing data, it belongs in the record. If losing it only means losing speed or fidelity, the agent can keep it.

Updates travel one way

Neither service mirrors the other, and only one direction carries updates.

A graph node broadcasts an event on its topic. The backend is subscribed, and its relay does two things with each event: writes down whatever belongs in the record, and fans the event out to the browser group. So the backend learns what happened by being told. It never reads the agent's tables, and the agent never writes to the backend's.

The useful consequence is that the record is derived, which means it can lag but it cannot diverge. A terminal event persists the turn. A parked run persists the approval card. A tool proposal is deliberately not persisted as a turn, because it only becomes one if it actually runs.

The place this shows up as real code is a small protocol on the backend describing everything the agent can announce:

class Sink:
    """Where a run's events are written down. Every hook is optional."""

    async def classified(self, category: str, priority: str, why: str) -> None: ...
    async def decided(self, decision: str, why: str) -> None: ...
    async def drafted(self, content: str, model: str) -> None: ...
    async def approval_required(self, draft: str, findings: list[str]) -> None: ...
    async def reply_sent(self, content: str) -> None: ...
    async def reply_blocked(self, findings: list[str]) -> None: ...
    async def token(self, delta: str) -> None: ...
    async def answered(self, content: str, model: str) -> None: ...
    async def tool_proposed(self, payload: Any) -> None: ...
    async def tool_ran(self, payload: Any) -> None: ...
    async def reasoning_delta(self, step: str, delta: str) -> None: ...
    async def reasoned(
        self, step: str, content: str, decision: str, model: str
    ) -> None: ...
    async def failed(self, message: str) -> None: ...

That interface is the boundary, written down. Three different callers open connections to the agent in this app: a ticket's customer-facing run, the same ticket's internal team run, and a standalone conversation. They turned out to differ only in what they wrote down, never in how they talked to the agent, so the talking lives in one place and the writing-down is whichever Sink you hand it. Every hook being optional is the bit that makes that work: a caller that does not care about token deltas simply does not implement token.

A boundary you can read in twenty lines is also a boundary you can test. Pass a recording Sink, drive the relay, and assert on what it would have written, with no database and no model.

The boundary is generated, not hand-written

Two services talking means a contract, and a hand-maintained contract between two codebases is a slow leak. I have watched a WebSocket message shape drift between a backend and a frontend that each believed they were right, and there is no satisfying way to debug it, because both sides are internally consistent.

So nothing here is hand-written. The agent's consumers produce an AsyncAPI document, and a generated Python client is what the backend imports:

from helpdesk.agent_client.agent_hub_support_topic.client import (
    AgentHubSupportTopicClient,
)
from helpdesk.agent_client.agent_hub_support_topic.messages import (
    ApprovalRequiredMessage,
    ReplySentMessage,
    RunRequestMessage,
    ToolApprovalMessage,
)

Change a message on the agent, regenerate, and the backend stops type-checking. That is the entire mechanism, and it is the same trick your REST API has had through OpenAPI for a decade. The next post covers how the generation works and what drift actually costs. For now the only claim is that the seam between two services is the last place you want a shape that exists only in two people's heads.

What it costs

Two services is more than one service, and I would rather say the costs out loud than discover them in your comments.

You now run two services locally, each with its own environment file and a shared token that has to match in both, plus a worker and the web app. The repo hides that behind a single setup command, but somebody wrote that command.

You have a network hop on the critical path. For this workload it disappears into model latency, which is measured in seconds, so a few milliseconds of local socket is noise. If your agent were doing something fast and chatty, the calculus would change.

You have a contract to regenerate. It is one command, but it is a step, and forgetting it produces a confusing failure until you learn the shape of it.

And you have two deploys, two sets of logs, and two things that can be down independently. Tracing across the boundary stops being free, which is a large part of why observability gets a post of its own rather than a paragraph.

When not to do this

I do not think this is unconditional. If you are building a prototype to find out whether an idea works, one service is correct, and splitting early is the kind of discipline that feels responsible while slowing you down for no return. The same goes for a tool with one user, which is you.

The signals that it is time: the model calls are slow enough that they are blocking your web workers; you want to scale the agent independently, or on different hardware; more than one person is working on the system and the prompts and the business rules are colliding in review; or you have started writing graph concepts into your application tables.

The reason to do it before you are forced to is simply that the cost curve is steep. Drawing the line while there is nothing across it is an afternoon. Drawing it after a year of leaks is the rewrite that gets postponed every quarter, and that one never gets cheaper.

Next up is types and contracts, which is the other idea the rest of the series leans on and the thing that makes this boundary enforceable rather than aspirational. Hope this one is useful if you are staring at a single service and wondering whether to cut it.

I write these deep-dives and maintain a handful of Python libraries, so if that is your kind of thing, follow along on GitHub and LinkedIn.

I do not think this is unconditional. If you are building a prototype to find out whether an idea works, one service is correct, and splitting early is the kind of discipline that feels responsible while slowing you down for no return. The same goes for a tool with one user, which is you.

The signals that it is time: the model calls are slow enough that they are blocking your web workers; you want to scale the agent independently, or on different hardware; more than one person is working on the system and the prompts and the business rules are colliding in review; or you have started writing graph concepts into your application tables.

The reason to do it before you are forced to is simply that the cost curve is steep. Drawing the line while there is nothing across it is an afternoon. Drawing it after a year of leaks is the rewrite that gets postponed every quarter, and that one never gets cheaper.

Next up is types and contracts, which is the other idea the rest of the series leans on and the thing that makes this boundary enforceable rather than aspirational. Hope this one is useful if you are staring at a single service and wondering whether to cut it.

I write these deep-dives and maintain a handful of Python libraries, so if that is your kind of thing, follow along on GitHub and LinkedIn.

title: Signing a PDF without printing it, and what that signature is not
summary:
The old routine for "sign and send this back" is print, sign with a pen, scan, email. For most everyday paperwork you can skip the printer. Before you do, it's worth knowing that "signing a PDF" means two very different things, because only one of them is something you can do with a picture of your signature.

Two things both called a signature

A visible mark. An image of your signature (drawn, typed in a script font, or photographed) placed on the page. It looks signed. To the file, it's just more page content, like a logo.

A digital signature. A certificate, a hash of the document's bytes, and a signature that a PDF reader can check. Acrobat and similar readers show these in a signature panel, and they tell you if the file changed after signing. Nothing about it depends on what the page looks like.

A landlord, a school, a club, or a colleague asking for "a signed copy" almost always means the first. If the instructions mention a digital signature certificate (DSC), a qualified or advanced electronic signature, or a specific signing platform, they mean the second. No image tool, command or script can turn a picture into that. You need a certificate from a provider or your organisation's signing service.

Built-in ways to place a visible mark

macOS Preview. Open the PDF, show the Markup toolbar, and use the Sign button. You can create a signature with the trackpad, the camera (hold your signature on paper up to it), or an iPhone, and Preview saves it for reuse. Click it to place it, then drag and resize.

Adobe Acrobat Reader (Windows and Mac). The free reader has a Fill & Sign tool. Add a signature there by typing, drawing, or choosing an image, then click where it goes.

Either way, keep the original file. Once the mark is saved into a copy, you can't cleanly take it back out.

Turning a photo of your signature into a clean PNG

If you'd rather use your real ink signature, sign a sheet of white paper, photograph it straight down in daylight, and crop roughly. The photo won't be white and black. Paper in a phone photo is light grey with a gradient, and that grey travels with the image.

This Pillow script turns everything darker than a cutoff into opaque black ink and everything else into transparent pixels, then trims the empty margin:

import sys
from PIL import Image, ImageOps

src, dst = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2]
cutoff = int(sys.argv[3]) if len(sys.argv) > 3 else 140   # 0-255, lower keeps less

gray = ImageOps.grayscale(Image.open(src))
# Ink becomes opaque black, paper becomes fully transparent.
alpha = gray.point(lambda v: 255 if v < cutoff else 0)
out = Image.new("RGBA", gray.size, (0, 0, 0, 0))
out.putalpha(alpha)
out = out.crop(alpha.getbbox())   # trim the empty margin
out.save(dst)
print(out.size)

python3 clean_signature.py signature-photo.jpg signature.png

On my test photo (900 x 360, grey paper getting lighter left to right, dark strokes) it produced a 766 x 178 RGBA PNG of 3,908 bytes. If faint parts of the stroke disappear, raise the cutoff. If paper texture or shadows show up as specks, lower it.

Stamping it onto a page from the command line

If you sign the same kind of document often, a script beats dragging things around. This one draws the PNG on a blank page of the same size with reportlab and lays that over the page you choose with pypdf (pip install pypdf reportlab):

import sys, io
from pypdf import PdfReader, PdfWriter
from reportlab.pdfgen import canvas

pdf_in, sig_png, pdf_out = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2], sys.argv[3]
page_no = int(sys.argv[4])               # 1-based
x, y, width = map(float, sys.argv[5:8])  # points from bottom-left; 72 pt = 1 inch

reader = PdfReader(pdf_in)
writer = PdfWriter(clone_from=reader)
page = writer.pages[page_no - 1]
pw, ph = float(page.mediabox.width), float(page.mediabox.height)

# Draw the PNG on a blank page of the same size, then lay it over the real page.
buf = io.BytesIO()
c = canvas.Canvas(buf, pagesize=(pw, ph))
c.drawImage(sig_png, x, y, width=width, preserveAspectRatio=True,
            anchor="sw", height=width, mask="auto")
c.save()
page.merge_page(PdfReader(buf).pages[0])
writer.write(pdf_out)

python3 stamp.py letter.pdf signature.png letter-signed.pdf 1 72 650 150

PDF coordinates start at the bottom-left corner, in points. An A4 page is about 595 x 842 points, so 72 650 is one inch from the left edge and a bit under a quarter of the way down from the top. 150 is the width of the mark in points, about 5.3 cm.

I checked the output three ways. The letter's text was still extractable as text after stamping, so the page wasn't flattened into a picture. Rendering the page with pdftoppm showed the signature sitting above the line with the text around it untouched. And the file went from 1,492 bytes to 5,739, since the PNG is small.

Checking which kind of signature a file has

pdfsig from poppler-utils lists the digital signatures in a PDF:

pdfsig letter-signed.pdf

For my stamped letter it printed File 'letter-signed.pdf' does not contain any signatures. That's the correct answer. The page has a mark, the file has no signature. Run it on a document you received with a real certificate signature and it lists the signer and whether the signature validates. It's a quick way to see which kind someone sent you, or which kind you're about to send.

Gotcha 1: a JPEG brings its paper with it

JPEG has no transparency. If you place the photo itself, you place a rectangle of grey paper. I stamped the original signature-photo.jpg at the same spot to compare: the grey box covered part of the "Yours faithfully," line above it, and the file grew to 42,120 bytes instead of 5,739. Use a PNG with a transparent background, like the one the script above makes.

Gotcha 2: adding a mark can break a signature that's already there

A digital signature covers a byte range of the file. If someone has already signed the document with a certificate and you add your mark with a tool that rewrites the whole file, like the script above, those bytes change and their signature stops validating. Acrobat avoids this by appending changes as an incremental update. If pdfsig shows an existing signature, add yours in a reader that preserves it, or ask the sender how they want it signed.

I built ToolOcean, a set of browser-based file tools. Its sign page places a drawn, typed or imported mark on one page in the browser tab, and says plainly that the result is not a certified or qualified signature: https://toolocean.co/pdf-sign
